title: Religious and Social Awakening in Colonial India
summary: Two major problems held back Indian society: lack of education and the subordination of women. Education was limited to a few upper-caste men; priests controlled the scriptures and imposed expensive rituals. Women suffered female infanticide, child marriage, polygamy and sati (a widow was compelled to burn herself on her husband's funeral pyre); they had no right to property or education. The caste system, originally based on occupation, had become hereditary and led to exploitation of the lower castes and untouchability.

Contact with Western ideas of liberty and equality and the criticism by Christian missionaries made reformers realise that ignorance and backwardness hindered progress. Since social practices were followed in the name of religion, they believed social reform was impossible without religious reform — hence 'socio-religious' movements. Reformers quoted the scriptures to show that evil practices had no religious sanction, and they promoted modern, scientific education, especially for women.

Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj (1828). Moved by his sister-in-law being forced to commit sati, he campaigned against it and Lord William Bentinck banned sati in 1829. He supported widow remarriage, opposed child marriage, idol worship and polytheism, believed in one God and the unity of religions, ran an English school in Calcutta, opened a Vedanta college (1825) and helped start the Hindu College. He represented a synthesis of Eastern and Western thought.

Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar's efforts led to the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act of 1856. He opposed child marriage and polygamy, helped open about 35 girls' schools in Bengal, brought Western thought into the Sanskrit College and opened it to non-Brahmin students.

Swami Dayanand Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in 1875. He held the Vedas to be infallible, wrote Satyarth Prakash, started the Shuddhi movement, fought untouchability and caste rigidity, preached in Hindi and inspired the D.A.V. (Dayanand Anglo-Vedic) schools and colleges.

Ramakrishna Paramhansa taught the unity of all religions. His disciple Swami Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission, stressed both spiritual and secular knowledge, self-confidence, removal of superstition, caste rigidity and untouchability, and the upliftment and education of women.

Sir Syed Ahmed Khan worked to remove the educational backwardness of Muslims: he opposed purdah, polygamy and easy divorce, opened an English school at Ghazipur (1864), founded the Mohammadan Anglo-Oriental (M.A.O.) College at Aligarh (1875) — later Aligarh Muslim University — a scientific society and the Mohammadan Educational Conference. This was the Aligarh Movement.

Jyotirao (Jyotiba) Phule and his wife Savitribai worked for women, peasants and lower castes; they opened a girls' school in 1848 and another in Poona in 1851, supported widow remarriage, and in September 1873 Phule formed the Satya Shodhak Samaj (Society of Seekers of Truth).

Justice M.G. Ranade founded the Prarthana Samaj (1867, Bombay) and the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha. Pandita Ramabai started the Arya Mahila Samaj (1881, Pune), the Mukti Mission (1889) for deserted widows and the Sharda Sadan. Annie Besant of the Theosophical Society came to India in 1893, became its President in 1907 and started the Central Hindu College at Banaras, which became part of Banaras Hindu University.

Other movements: Abdul Latif's Mohammedan Literary Society of Calcutta (1863); Shariatullah's Faraizi movement; Mirza Ghulam Ahmed's Ahmadiya Movement (1899); the poet Muhammad Iqbal ('Saare jahan se achcha'); the Singh Sabhas at Amritsar and Lahore (1870s) and Khalsa College (1892) among the Sikhs, and the Akali movement (1920) which, after a satyagraha against corrupt mahants, won the Gurdwara Act of 1925; and Parsi reformers (Dadabhai Naoroji and others) who founded the Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha in 1851.

The movements spread rational, scientific and humanitarian thinking, criticised caste and untouchability, and improved the status of women: sati and infanticide were made illegal, widow remarriage allowed (1856), inter-caste marriage allowed (1872) and child marriage restricted by the Sharda Act (1929: girls 14, boys 18). They gave Indians self-respect, self-confidence and pride in their country, and created the national consciousness that led to the freedom struggle; many women took part in it. Limitation: they reached mainly the educated few, not the masses of peasants and urban poor.

Identify the person: (a) He and his wife Savitribai Phule are most known for their efforts to educate women, the lower castes and the masses. (b) He founded the Mohammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh.
(a) Jyotirao (Jyotiba) Phule (b) Sir Syed Ahmed Khan
Answer briefly: (a) Why did Raja Ram Mohan Roy oppose Sati Pratha? (b) Why did Swami Dayanand Saraswati found the Arya Samaj?

(a) He was moved by his brother's widow being forced to commit sati; it was inhuman and, as he showed from the scriptures, had no sanction in Hindu religion. (b) To reform Hindu religion on the basis of the Vedas and to fight superstition, untouchability and caste rigidity in North India.
vsa: Describe any two endeavours of Raja Rammohan Roy in the field of social reform.

(1) He campaigned against sati, citing scriptures to show it had no religious sanction; with Lord Bentinck's support it was banned in 1829. (2) He advocated widow remarriage, opposed child marriage and idol worship, and promoted English and scientific education (English school in Calcutta, Hindu College).

or: Explain any two endeavours of Jyotirao Govindrao Phule.

(1) He and Savitribai Phule opened schools for girls (1848, and in Poona in 1851) and educated women and lower castes. (2) In 1873 he founded the Satya Shodhak Samaj to free the lower castes from exploitation; he also promoted widow remarriage.

vsa: Mention any two reforms brought by Swami Dayanand Saraswati in the field of education.

(1) He preached in Hindi so that ideas reached ordinary people of North India. (2) His followers started the D.A.V. (Dayanand Anglo-Vedic) schools and colleges which taught English and modern science along with Sanskrit and Vedic learning.
Who founded the Brahmo Samaj? Mention any two of its principles.

Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded it in 1828. Principles: (1) worship of one God (monotheism) and opposition to idol worship and meaningless rituals; (2) unity of all religions and opposition to social evils like sati and child marriage.
Why did reformers feel that social reform had no meaning without religious reform?

Most evil social practices like sati, untouchability and child marriage were followed in the name of religion and supported by priests. So reformers first showed from the scriptures that these practices had no religious sanction, and then tried to change society.
Write any two limitations of the reform movements.

(1) They affected only a small percentage of the population, mostly the educated class. (2) They could not reach the vast masses of peasants and the urban poor, who continued to live in the same conditions.
sa: Who introduced English education among the Muslims? Explain his contribution in this area.

Sir Syed Ahmed Khan. (1) He believed only modern Western education could bring Muslims progress and advocated English despite orthodox opposition. (2) He opened an English school at Ghazipur (1864) and founded the M.A.O. College at Aligarh (1875), which became Aligarh Muslim University. (3) He set up a scientific society to translate English books, published a journal and started the Mohammadan Educational Conference — the Aligarh Movement.

Explain the contribution of Swami Dayanand Saraswati in reforming Hindu religion in India.

He founded the Arya Samaj in 1875, held the Vedas infallible and rejected ideas against them, wrote Satyarth Prakash and started the Shuddhi movement. He opposed idol worship, untouchability and caste rigidity, worked to improve women's condition, used Hindi to reach the people and inspired the D.A.V. schools; the Arya Samaj also built self-respect and self-reliance that helped the national movement.

Explain the contribution of Swami Vivekananda in the religious and social reform movement in India.

He spread the teachings of Ramakrishna Paramhansa about the unity of religions and founded the Ramakrishna Mission. He stressed that Indians needed both spiritual and secular knowledge and faith in themselves. He fought superstition, caste rigidity and untouchability, worked for women's upliftment and education, and gave primary importance to removing ignorance.

Why was Jyotirao Govindrao Phule considered an eminent reformer?

(1) He fought for equal rights for peasants and lower castes. (2) With Savitribai Phule he started schools for girls and educated women and the masses. (3) He promoted widow remarriage. (4) He founded the Satya Shodhak Samaj (1873) to protect lower castes from exploitation and atrocities.

(2) Laws were passed against sati and infanticide, for widow remarriage (1856) and inter-caste marriage (1872), and against child marriage (1929); women's education spread. la: How did the socio-religious reform movements lead to the Indian National Movement? Explain in six points.

(1) They gave Indians self-respect, self-confidence and pride in their culture and country. (2) They spread rational and scientific thinking and modern education, producing an educated class aware of liberty and equality. (3) By attacking caste, untouchability and religious divisions they promoted social unity. (4) Better status and education brought women into public life and the freedom struggle (Sarojini Naidu, Aruna Asaf Ali, Laxmi Sehgal). (5) Organisations like the Arya Samaj and Theosophical Society built self-reliance and political awakening. (6) People became conscious of their identity as Indians, which led to a united struggle against the British; after 1919 the national movement itself carried forward social reform.

or: Who introduced English education among the Muslims? Explain in six points his contribution.

Sir Syed Ahmed Khan. (1) He believed Muslims could progress only through modern Western scientific knowledge. (2) He advocated learning English despite opposition from orthodox Muslims. (3) He opened an English school at Ghazipur in 1864. (4) He founded the M.A.O. College at Aligarh in 1875, teaching humanities and science through English; it became Aligarh Muslim University. (5) He set up a scientific society to translate English books and published a journal for reform. (6) He started the Mohammadan Educational Conference and worked for women's education against purdah and polygamy — the Aligarh Movement.

la: Explain the social practices that existed in 19th-century India and how reformers fought them.

(1) Female infanticide was common; it was later made illegal. (2) Child marriage was widespread; reformers opposed it and the Sharda Act (1929) fixed minimum ages. (3) Sati: Raja Ram Mohan Roy campaigned and it was banned in 1829. (4) Widows lived miserable lives; Vidyasagar's efforts produced the Widow Remarriage Act (1856), and Pandita Ramabai's Mukti Mission sheltered them. (5) Polygamy and purdah were opposed by Vidyasagar and Sir Syed. (6) Rigid caste and untouchability were attacked by the Arya Samaj, Phule's Satya Shodhak Samaj, Vivekananda and others; education, especially for girls, was the main tool of change.
